sentences.text: Cedarpelta was a large ankylosaur estimated to reach a length of 7 meters and a mass of 5 tonnes.
Unlike most relatives, its individual skull bones were not completely fused, and adult skulls lacked a distinctive pattern of fused head tiles.
Two skulls are known, with an estimated cranial length of roughly 60 centimeters.
The upper jaw possessed six conical teeth, while the maxilla contained eighteen teeth.
Researchers proposed that skull armor formed in an intermediate layer called the periosteum rather than directly from the skin or skull bones.
No tail club or mace is known for this animal, suggesting early ankylosaurs might have lacked a true tail club.
Fossils were discovered by Evan Hall and Sue Ann Bilbey near the Price River in Carbon County, Utah.
The genus was named in 2001 by Kenneth Carpenter, James Kirkland, Don Burge, and John Bird, with the specific name honoring the discoverers.
The animal exhibits the closure of the lateral temporal fenestra, an advanced trait found only in ankylosaurids.
One skull was found disarticulated, providing the first opportunity to examine individual ankylosaurid skull bones rather than a fused unit.
Carpenter classified the taxon within the family Ankylosauridae.
Vickaryous and colleagues interpreted the genus as the most basal member of the family Nodosauridae, placed below Pawpawsaurus, Silvisaurus, and Sauropelta.
However, new skeletal material confirmed Carpenter's original identification that Cedarpelta is one of the most basal ankylosaurs.
Cedarpelta lived in Utah during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically between 98.2 and 93 million years ago.
The fossils are now assigned to the base of the Mussentuchit Member, dating between 116 and 109 million years ago at the Aptian-Albian boundary.
Cedarpelta lived from the Aptian to the Albian stages, between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago.
Researchers have debated whether Cedarpelta represents the most basal known ankylosaurid or if it formed an early ankylosaurid clade called Shamosaurinae alongside Gobisaurus and Shamosaurus.
